title: Britain must not rely on foreign AI, says former military intelligence chief
content:
Britain must not rely on foreign AI, says former military intelligence chief
Britain must not rely on foreign AI, a former military intelligence chief has warned.
Gen Sir Jim Hockenhull, who was head of Cyber and Specialist Operations Command (CSOC) until June, urged the Government to exercise extreme caution when relying on AI contracts obtained abroad as Russia becomes more aggressive in its hybrid attacks on Britain.
He said: "The world has rarely felt less safe."
Writing for The Telegraph (see below) in his first comments since leaving the Armed Services after a 40-year career, Gen Hockenhull warned that hostile states were launching attacks through cyberspace, disinformation, sponsoring terrorism and conducting espionage and sabotage "on a scale not seen before".
He said that while AI would "redefine warfare" and provide many benefits for Britain, including affording military analysts "greater speed and accuracy", it couldalso "leave the UK more exposed to cyber-attack".
"A technology that helps the defender also helps the attacker," he wrote, as he stressed the need to understand any AI models used in military planning and intelligence analysis.
In September, The Telegraph revealed that, over the past five years, more than £30bn of UK defence contracts have been awarded to foreign suppliers, despite being counted as domestic spending.
Thousands of contracts that ministers claimed had been awarded in the UK had in fact been given to companies headquartered offshore.
Data obtained under freedom of information laws that show that ministers have awarded £31.7bn in defence contracts to foreign-controlled firms with UK offices since 2021, compared with £3.5bn spent with foreign suppliers without a presence in Britain.
Gen Hockenhull, who has been made president of the British technology startup Valarian, warned that Britain's dependence on foreign AI was deepening.
"Five companies control 70 per cent of global AI compute, none of them British," the four-star general said.
"We must not be a high-value AI customer. A state that runs its tax system, its intelligence analysis and military planning on models owned, hosted and updated abroad is not master of its own house.
"It is a tenant, and tenants can be evicted, repriced or spied upon. This is a critical vulnerability, especially so in time of crisis."
As head of CSOC, previously called Strategic Command, Gen Hockenhull held one of the most senior jobs in the Armed Forces, overseeing UK special forces, Defence Intelligence, National Cyber Force and Permanent Joint Headquarters.
In the role, he saw up close how hostile states were "attacking infrastructure through cyberspace, running information operations, sponsoring terrorism and conducting espionage and sabotage on a scale not seen before".
"Modern conflict is no longer confined to the battlefield – it is not constrained by lines on maps," he said. "It runs through cables, across the electromagnetic spectrum, in data centres and supply chains. And it is under way long before anyone declares war."
Gen Hockenhull said four things were required to regain control of the situation, which included the Government inspecting and testing any systems it uses, ensuring sensitive data sit on infrastructure it trusts, not being held "hostage" by relying on single suppliers, or foreign governments, and had to have the skills to be self-sufficient.
He said that Britain should not be timid in its approach to working with AI, but it had to "own the keys" while doing so.
Britain must own the keys to AI
by Gen Sir Jim Hockenhull
The world has rarely felt less safe. Those who run Britain's Armed Forces and Civil Service, usually a cautious lot in public, now speak in unusually plain terms about the threats we face.
Hostile states are attacking infrastructure through cyberspace, running information operations, sponsoring terrorism and conducting espionage and sabotage on a scale not seen before.
Modern conflict is no longer confined to the battlefield – it is not constrained by lines on maps. It runs through cables, across the electromagnetic spectrum, in data centres and supply chains. And it is under way long before anyone declares war.
Into this world a technology of startling promise has arrived. AI will transform our lives. It will redefine warfare and may prove the deepest shift in how states are governed. The evidence is already visible. HMRC has used machine learning to protect and recover £10bn in a single year, and AI is helping to halve decision times on routine householder planning applications.
The same logic applies to defence. AI gives military analysts greater speed and accuracy, sifting surveillance data that no human team could read. It helps make faster and better decisions and is vital in augmenting other new technologies. In a nation with tight budgets, a shrinking pool of talent and a long list of threats, a technology that multiplies the output of each person must be exploited.
But a technology that helps the defender also helps the attacker. Officials have been candid that an AI-enabled state could leave the UK more exposed to cyber-attack.
The more Whitehall rebuilds its workflows around AI, the more those systems become a prize. Defence chiefs add that adversaries will use AI to degrade British capabilities, and that the military must understand how AI is working when it enters decision-making chains. A model that cannot be explained cannot be trusted as part of life-or-death judgment, and one that cannot be audited cannot be trusted with a welfare payment either.
Here, sovereignty stops being a slogan. Britain's dependence is deep and getting deeper. Five companies control 70 per cent of global AI compute, none of them British. We must not be a high-value AI customer. A state that runs its tax system, its intelligence analysis and military planning on models owned, hosted and updated abroad is not master of its own house. It is a tenant, and tenants can be evicted, repriced or spied upon. This is a critical vulnerability, especially so in a time of crisis.
Sovereignty need not mean autarky. The Government is right to stress that it is not a call for isolationism or for going it alone. Britain will never build every chip or train every frontier model, and it would be foolish to try. The aim is narrower and more achievable: control over what the country cannot afford to lose.
That means four things. The Government must be able to inspect and test the systems it uses. Its sensitive data must sit on infrastructure it can trust; this is equally true for any company or organisation that wants to retain control. It needs credible alternatives, so no single supplier, or foreign government, can hold it hostage. And it must have the skills to do all this itself.
The last necessity is the scarcest. A new AI-focused intake for the Civil Service's graduate scheme is welcome. But Whitehall alone cannot buy its way to sovereignty, and it cannot hire its way there on Civil Service pay scales alone.
It will need partnerships with British firms, universities and like-minded allies, and the nerve to back domestic champions before they are obviously safe bets.
Nothing here argues for caution about AI. The costs of timidity are as real as the risks of haste: slower services, weaker defences and a nation that lags behind our competitors and our adversaries. But speed without control is merely dependence at a higher tempo. Britain should adopt AI boldly. It must insist, just as boldly, on owning the keys.
Gen Sir Jim Hockenhull is a former commander of Cyber and Specialist Operations Command and is now president of Valarian Technologies

report.summary: Former UK cyber commander Gen Sir Jim Hockenhull warns Britain must cut reliance on foreign AI models and infrastructure to protect sovereignty and security.
report.background: Britain's defence and public-sector AI dependence has become a national-security debate after disclosures that £31.7bn in defence contracts since 2021 went to foreign-controlled firms with UK offices. The warning comes as Russia and other hostile states intensify hybrid attacks—cyber operations, disinformation, espionage and sabotage—and as AI spreads into military planning, intelligence analysis and tax administration. Global AI compute is highly concentrated: five companies control about 70%, none British. The UK has strong AI research and startup pockets but relies on US hyperscalers and frontier models for advanced capabilities. Government policy stresses AI adoption but has not resolved how to keep sensitive data, decision chains and critical infrastructure under trusted control.
key_points: Hockenhull calls foreign AI dependence a 'critical vulnerability': if tax systems, intelligence analysis or military planning run on models owned, hosted and updated abroad, the UK is a tenant that can be evicted, repriced or spied on in a crisis.

AI is dual-use. It speeds military analysis and public services, but also helps attackers and creates new targets. Models entering life-or-death or welfare decisions must be explainable and auditable; if officials cannot understand or inspect a model, they cannot trust it.

The market is concentrated: five firms control 70% of global AI compute, none British, and foreign suppliers dominate recent UK defence contracts. Hockenhull says Britain must not be merely a high-value AI customer and needs credible alternatives to avoid being held hostage by one supplier or government.

He proposes four sovereignty tests: government can inspect and test systems; sensitive data sits on trusted infrastructure; there are alternative suppliers; and the UK has homegrown skills. Sovereignty is not autarky—Britain need not build every chip or model, but must control what it cannot afford to lose.

Whitehall cannot buy or hire its way to sovereignty alone. Hockenhull urges partnerships with British firms, universities and allies, plus willingness to back domestic AI champions before they are safe bets. He argues for bold adoption paired with equally bold insistence on 'owning the keys'.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this signals a likely shift from cheapest-compliant procurement toward sovereign, auditable and resilient AI. Expect demand for data residency, local inference, model transparency, supply-chain security and multi-vendor architectures. Developers may face new assurance requirements—documentation, red-teaming, explainability and exit plans—but also opportunities in open-weight models and UK-based infrastructure. For regular users, public-service AI should become more accountable and less exposed to foreign shutdowns or data access, though tighter rules could slow some deployments and raise costs. The bigger lesson is that AI sovereignty is becoming a procurement and engineering problem, not just a geopolitical slogan.
report.tools: To follow sovereign-AI themes, try open-weight models (Llama, Mistral, Qwen) with Ollama or vLLM, and llama.cpp for local inference. Hugging Face Transformers supports self-hosting; SHAP, Captum and LIME help model auditability; Sigstore and SLSA harden software supply chains. Kubernetes or OpenStack can support trusted data infrastructure. Watch the UK AI Safety Institute's evaluations and Valarian's work.
